notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1094.tmp1094.opp-lat: Ch. 1: 'Si quis ii dei' – the stray 'ii' is likely a scanning artefact, omitted. 'praeposito' rendered 'prior'. Ch. 4: 'quire' read as 'choro'. Ch. 7: 'periods' read as 'personis'. Ch. 8: the passage on the ploughman, reaper and vinedresser echoes Jerome, Letter 46. Ch. 3: 'spiritual father' presumably means acting as godfather (sponsor); the sense is uncertain.

XIII: 'funi contagio' read as 'furti contagio' (contagion of theft). The scriptural reference '(Ephes. ii)' attached to the Cyprian quotation appears misplaced. XVI: 'inaequalitate constricti' is probably a corruption of 'infirmitate constricti' (constrained by sickness); translated so. XII: 'cenis quibus ue temporibus' read as 'certis quibusque temporibus'. Other evident scanning errors (e.g. 'iota' for 'tota', 'ni' for 'ne', 'dimiserim' for 'dimiserint') silently corrected.

Evident scanning errors read as: Cum for 'Gum', faciet inspectore for 'faciei in- spectore', expetierint for 'expetierim', vitium for 'vilium', praepositum for 'propositum', proficere for 'prolicere', vos for 'jos', vestris for 'ventris', vestrum for 'vestium', deesse for 'desse'. Ch. XVIII: 'statuatis' (resolve) may stand for 'dicatis' (say); 'cupiditatis vitio' (vice of desire) reads oddly where the context concerns the wanton eye. Ch. XIX: the sentences 'et ita sunt indigentibus tribuenda, ne vitio avaritiae reservatae, providendis singulis detur audacia' and 'Si quis vero his negligenter expetenda putaverit' are obscure and probably corrupt; the renderings are tentative. Ch. XXII: 'quantum desiderant non possunt humiliari personas' is rendered as it stands; the sense seems to be that superiors cannot humble themselves as much as they would wish. Biblical references are given as printed in the edition; several are inexact (e.g. 'Ephes. iv' for the yes/no saying, 'Luc. xvii' for Luke 10:16).

nodes.text: THE RULE OF THE MONASTERY OF TARNANT.

Chapter One. If anyone, set on fire with the ardour of God, renouncing the world, has chosen with great deliberation to seek a monastery, his newness should not at once be granted permission to enter; but first it should be inquired into with special care whether he has come willingly or compelled by some necessity, or whether he is held bound by any condition of servitude. When this has reached the abbot's knowledge through the report of the prior, he should be assigned to one of the seniors and ordered to serve those who arrive for as long as it takes until his devotion has been shown, with patience as its witness. Next, he should be instructed in the disciplines of the rule and learn what he must do and whom it is fitting for him to serve; then the whole ordinance of the rule should be read over to him, and to test his obedience harsh and rough commands should be given him, and he is to keep nothing as his own property of those things he brought with him. But if his vow is such that he wishes to give what is his to the uses of the monastery, let sincere devotion commend his offering in full, and let him place it upon the altar; from which to demand anything back is judged sacrilege. If, when about to move to the monastery, he has brought livestock of any kind, he should receive the price from the abbot, and he is not to be refused [leave] to do what he wishes with that price. If the abbot does not wish to buy them, he should be allowed to sell them to whomever he wishes; or, which is better, let him entrust them to the prior to be sold; but the price itself, as has already been said, is to be disbursed by him whose property it had been, provided that nothing remains in his possession. For it is wrong that one who intends to escape the snare of this world should keep back something by which the devil's assault could entangle him. If he brings with him a client, a servant, or a relative, and [that person] asks to be admitted into the fellowship of religion, it is fitting that he be tested by a similar examination and joined to the brothers; and one who had formerly been subject to him in servitude is to be counted a brother, placed in the service of the Lord, because with God, as the Apostle teaches, there is no respect of persons (Col. 3). Yet the one who from a humble condition has been received into the equality of brotherhood should not grow proud with any swelling of conceit; but through humility let the good things in him grow strong; and not only to the one to whom he has been made equal, but to the whole brotherhood, as a true servant of Christ, let him give service with devotion and humility. For just as the one who seemed greater in the world is, through the disposition of humility, called a brother from the Lord, so the other, mindful of himself, should not despise his condition by seeking higher things, but exalt it by the witness of humility, so that he may find grace with God. And no one is permitted to change his habit until a year has been completed. But if the compunction of the one asking is so great that he demands by constant supplication that this not be refused him, what is granted to one person asking faithfully is not to be held as if it were permitted [to all]. Also the clothes brought with him, which the use of the first year cannot wear out, are to be turned into money and given to whomever the abbot orders; because when he has earned other garments, his former clothing will not be in his control, so that the change of the outer man may fully accord with the progress of the inner. He is not permitted to exchange any of the things he receives, neither for poorer ones out of self-abasement nor for better ones for comfort, but whatever kind are allotted, he shall claim them, with thanksgiving, only for his own use.

Chapter II. No one is allowed to choose a separate dwelling, nor is he permitted to claim as his own a little cupboard or anything similar that can be locked privately. He should not set out on a journey alone, unless accompanied by the company of a brother. On returning, they should not dare to report the things they have seen done outside, except only those that edify the hearers. When a senior is present, a junior should be wary of bursting out in presumptuous talkativeness; but, as often happens, if the senior is of a rather simple nature, then the junior should carry out what has been commanded him. On any feast day it will not be permitted to seek out a celebrated monk unless allowed, because the Lord, as the Gospel attests, promised that he would hear openly the one who prays in secret (Matt. 6).

Chapter III. If anyone is sent by the brothers on any business to a city, a fort, or a village at a senior's command, he should not presume to go anywhere except to the one to which he is directed. He should by no means consent to become a spiritual father without the abbot's command; but if a cause of great necessity arises, or, swayed by the entreaties of some faithful person, he cannot escape what is forbidden, then what is known to have been imposed on him against his protest must by all means be accepted out of regard for charity.

Chapter IV. Conversations with a woman from outside without witnesses are forbidden by the lawful authority of the canons; and they are by no means to be allowed to join privately in talk even with mothers and sisters, lest these overthrow, through worldly presumption, those set in the very newness of their service. And no one should go off anywhere without permission granted by a senior. Nor should he presume to take a boat across to the far bank without a senior's command; nor cut his hair and beard, or dare to make a cord or anything else, unless a senior's leave allows it. In the evening and night hours when the other brothers are resting, whoever is found absent from his dwelling or his bed should be punished, the seniors rebuking him; and when placed in the choir, one should not speak to another.

Chapter V. Whoever, when the signal is given, comes late to the Work of God or to any work whatever, should be shut out and put to shame for the guilt of so great an offence. And for any fault, however harsh the reproof with which he is rebuked, he should judge it wrong to answer back to the one who reproves him, but by humbling himself should show that amendment of the fault will follow; because God has promised that he will give grace to the humble (1 Pet. 5). With one who is removed from the fellowship of prayer or of the table for a fault committed, no one should dare to converse, except the one who can sweeten the bitterness of the expelled brother by mingling in teaching and charity.

Chapter VI. At vigils, while the readings are being read to all sitting, or when they are intent on prayer, no one should think he has been given leave to come in or go out. But whoever is compelled by the cause of common necessity may leave while the others are chanting psalms, without fear of any guilt, to return at once to the work in hand. And whoever presumes to chatter while others are praying or chanting psalms should not doubt that he is guilty not only before the brotherhood but also before the Godhead. Care must also be taken that idle hands do not invite sleep; and therefore the works to be done at vigils will be such as do not occupy the mind or burden the worker's hearing, but can drive off the torpor of drowsiness. But nothing is to be put before prayer and the word of God. On the Lord's night, however, out of reverence for the Lord's resurrection, manual work should cease; which it is fitting to observe also on certain solemn feasts.

Chapter VII. While the brothers are meditating, no one is allowed to busy himself with other things; nor should he think himself free to leave the school or the place where the brothers meditate. Whoever bursts out into this presumption will be subject to excommunication, as is fitting. It is unlawful to enter another's cell, except for the abbot and the prior, unless a signal has been given; because to them alone is it granted to know the secrets of the brothers and to search out by hidden inspection how each conducts himself. And no one should presume to approach where the craftsmen work, except the persons named above. To those who arrive, too, the junior will show nothing but a disposition of humility and due service, and he should not presume to concern himself with the reason for which [the visitor] came or when he will return, because the care of the seniors, not the presumption of the juniors, ought to inquire into this.

Chapter VIII. A junior should not dare to rebuke a senior; but if he knows something is being done or has been done outside the rule, it must be reserved for the abbot or the prior, so that what is reproved may be corrected by the correction of the rule. Whatever is committed by anyone without witnesses, if it comes to the abbot's knowledge, should be amended privately; if it has become known to all, the one guilty of the offence committed should be reproved before all. Whoever confesses in private the assaults of his thoughts for the sake of his own comfort should not be despised nor exposed to others, but as far as possible cherished with gentle exhortation. Whoever speaks unsuitably while others are chanting psalms in private meditation should be reproved according to the rule. In whatever work, then, they will either meditate on what is holy, or else keep silent. At table especially no one should presume to speak except one who has been questioned. What is needed for food it is fitting for the prior to recognise, and whatever is lacking according to custom he should order to be supplied quietly. Sitting at table, let them listen in silence to the reading that is being read; but if there is no reader present, let meditation on the holy Scriptures be chewed over like food, so that the body does not alone receive food, but the hungry soul too is fed with the word of God. Devote yourselves to prayers at the appointed hours and times; when the Lord is entreated with psalms and hymns, let what is uttered by the voice be planted in the heart. Let the ploughman holding the plough-handle sing Alleluia; let the sweating reaper divert himself with psalms; and while the vinedresser prunes the curved vine-shoot with his hook, let him sing something of David. Let these be your songs; these, as people commonly say, your love songs; these the shepherds' piping; these the tools of your cultivation. Let monks have no care for the things that the men of this world do; but let the meditation of their heart be intent on the fear of the Lord.

Chapter IX. At all times they will devote two hours a day to spiritual meditation. In summer, once matins have been completed as usual and prime said, all should take up the work they are ordered to do. Then, when terce has been celebrated, they should go back to finish what they had undertaken; and they should not be occupied in conversation about any worldly tales, unless perhaps the speaker brings out something that may edify the soul of the hearer. From the sixth hour until the ninth they should also be free for rest or even for reading. After the ninth hour, either in the garden or wherever need requires, all will lend their help together until the hour of the lamp-lighting. In winter, once matins and prime have been completed, all are allowed to devote themselves to reading until terce. When that is over, they should hasten gladly to carry out what has been enjoined on them, as has already been said, until the hour of the lamp-lighting. Those, however, who are seen to be assigned to cultivating the land cannot be bound by this observance, because of the constancy of their work; but as the season demands, or as their labour shows the work enjoined, so let them be governed by the judgement of the prior, while they too will nonetheless devote two hours to reading. When the harvests and vintages are being gathered, they should take a meal twice a day, that is, at the sixth hour and the twelfth. On the fourth and sixth days of the week, however, they ought to regulate their work so that, if it can be done, they do not omit the appointed fasts. But all things should be arranged by the senior's judgement, as need or labour demands. Yet no one should eat or drink outside the monastery: for the discipline of the Rule does not allow even cheap fruit to be taken; they should not presume to drink even water before the lawful meal.

Chapter X. When they make bread, or in any bodily task, they will relieve one another's labour; and however intent they may seem on any work, they should not omit the times of praying and chanting psalms, so that while they choose to prepare fleshly food, they may be fed spiritually by the word of God and by the meditation of a good conscience. From this work, however, it is fitting that no one be absent except one whom sickness holds back, or whom the prior has ordered to be occupied in some other matter. To the cellar should be appointed, by the abbot's judgement or the counsel of the seniors, such a man as considers not the wishes of some but the needs of all, with fear of the Lord and love of the brothers; to him, in the prior's absence, harmonious obedience should be given, and where need requires, help should not be refused.

Chapter XI. The stewards of the monastery ought to be chosen or appointed from such as are proved to edify others by the example of their life, and who keep with the greatest care, out of fear of the Lord, the alms assigned to the monastery or the things collected by the brothers. For if one neglects to keep the property of the servants of God entrusted to him, as one of the Fathers says, he wrongs God, and if he squanders it he will have to render account to the Lord. Whatever is given to them for the love of God should be added to the monastery's offering and benefit the whole community. We who desire to choose the apostolic life, why should we claim as our own what we know will shortly perish?

Chapter XII. The gardener ought to be so appointed that he is supported by the help of both the prior and the cellarer. And since the expenses of the cellar are aided by the benefit of vegetables, they ought to be both spent and cultivated according to the cellarer's management. It is fitting too that all iron tools and other implements be kept by both persons, yet so that each keeps what has been consigned to him with diligence and the greatest care; and no one should presume to take from another's store-room what does not belong to him without the consent of the one into whose charge it has been given. Whoever presumes to do this on his own wicked authority, since he does not fear to create scandals over the smallest things, should be shown to be guilty before the whole community for neglecting the Rule. Nor should anyone choose for himself the day's work to be done; this must rest in the senior's decision, so that he orders to be done by his judgement what he sees to be useful. No one should do anything grumbling, lest he share the end of those whose example he follows. No one is allowed to visit his relatives too often; yet to a person who is proved to be concerned for the salvation of his kin, access for visiting may be allowed at certain times. It is fitting, however, that he guard vigorously against the snare of the world, lest while he thinks he can win others, he make himself a stranger to the Lord.

Chapter XIII. No one should go to a wedding feast, lest through the wantonness of worldly people he come to know the things of the world, and, God forbid, be called back to the life of this world, if not in body then in mind, as the most blessed Cyprian said: adultery is learned while it is seen. Whoever presumes to bring out anything jocular or fit for laughter in the gathering of the brothers, or whoever wishes to tell idle tales with the juniors, or to have friendships with those of a weak age, will be subject to rebuke, as he deserves. If anyone finds anything, he should not conceal what he found, nor hide what ought to be made known. If he is convicted of having kept what was found for the space of one day, he should know that he is stained with the contagion of theft. If anyone learns that someone, not bearing the strictness of the monastery, is planning to flee, and does not at once report it, he should not doubt that he shares in that man's perdition; and he is to be separated from the gathering of the brothers for as long as it takes until that man can be called back. If anyone does not strive with all his strength to keep these things, which will please the Lord, and once and a second time rebuked does not amend, it is fitting that the faults be punished according to the measure of his age.

Chapter XIV. These are the things established in the monastery which it is fitting to observe for the love and fear of God. Since you have been gathered into one for the fear of the Lord, you ought to dwell of one mind in the house of the Lord, and you should have one soul and one heart, watchful in the fear of the Lord; and you should consider that you have nothing of your own, but all things should be common to you, to be distributed to you by the abbot's command, not equally to all, but as the principle of distribution or the cause of sickness requires; yet to each should be given according to his need, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: that they had all things in common, and distribution was made to each as each had need (Acts 4). Those who had something in the world, when they are found worthy to seek the monastery, should gladly hand it over to benefit all, striving that when they have given up their wealth, they at the same time strip off the very will to covet; and when the possession is given up, the passion too should be cast off. As for those who had nothing, it is shameful for them to seek what they do not recall having left behind. And they should not think themselves fortunate because they have found in the monastery what they could not find outside; nor should they be proud that they are joined with those whom before they could not approach because of the abundance of their riches or the splendour of their birth; but they should keep their hearts lifted up, and not seek things that are transient or will perish in swift course. Where the rich are humbled, the poor should not be puffed up, lest monasteries begin to be more useful to the rich than to the needy. And those who seemed wealthy in the world should not receive with disdain brothers who come to the holy fellowship out of poverty, but should rejoice in the fellowship and shared life of such persons. Nor should they be exalted if they have contributed some small portion of their means to help the expenses of the brotherhood, and so afterwards fall from the very point from which they first desired to ascend. What good is it to scatter riches and become poor by giving to the poor, if the wretched soul becomes prouder by despising riches than it had been by possessing them? All of you, then, persevering in unanimity, honour in yourselves God, whose temples you have been found worthy to become. First of all let us love God with the whole strength of the mind, then our neighbour: for these are the commandments given specially to us. To the abbot, after God, honour should be paid and reverence kept; to the prior, as befits a servant of God, full love and harmonious obedience should be given.

Chapter XV. In the oratory nothing at all should be done except the service of praying and chanting psalms, so that the works constantly done there may agree with its name; so that if anyone comes in outside the appointed hours to make supplication to the Lord, another's occupation does not hinder his prayer. Do not sing anything except what you read is to be sung. Mortify your flesh through abstinence, tame it with fasts and vigils; but wash your soul clean with the brightness of a good way of life.

Chapter XVI. If a brother worn down by abstinence cannot bear the fasts undertaken, he should still consider it unseemly to take anything before the hour of the midday meal has come. But those who are held back by illness and cannot keep the appointed hours should lawfully be allowed to eat when they can. Nor ought it to cause annoyance to others if more generous food is provided for those who in their worldly life were treated more lavishly; and those whom either modesty of birth or other habits make stronger should not for this reason think themselves seen as more blessed. Nor should they judge those more fortunate to whom in sickness is given what is withdrawn from the healthy for the rigour of observance; and if food or clothing is given more generously to those whom their parents raised more delicately, the brotherhood ought not to be disturbed because what is denied to those stronger in body by the rule's ordinance is granted to these out of consideration of charity: for regard ought to be had to how much they have despised out of love of religion, and to what lowliness they have submitted themselves by divine inspiration. Nor should the above-mentioned allowance granted to a few be regarded by the whole community as if it were a rule. For it is not fair that in a blessed dwelling, where the rich bow down, the poor should be raised up. Certainly those constrained by sickness are to be so treated that generous provision may more swiftly restore strength worn down by illness; and for those remaining in sickness the difference between persons should not bring about distinctions in food. Yet when they have regained the full strength of the body, they should be held by the customary reins of abstinence; for it befits the servants of God not to lessen the habit of good work, but to increase it.

Chapter XVII. Your habit should not be conspicuous, and you should not aim to please by your clothes, but by your conduct. When you go out, walk together. When you have arrived at the place you wished to reach, under the Lord's protection, the whole brotherhood should stay together in one place. In walking, in standing, in every movement of the body, nothing unseemly should be seen that might offend the gaze of anyone watching; but give your attention to those things that befit your holiness.

Chapter XVIII. If your eyes, turned in any direction, fall upon the faces of women, yet your mind, given to God, should not be polluted by any stain of desire. So when you go out, since you are not forbidden, and are not able, to avoid the sight of women, yet to desire them, or to wish to be desired by them, is a crime. Desire for women is incurred not by touch and feeling alone, but also by looking: and do not resolve that you have chaste eyes if you bear unchaste minds, for an unchaste eye is the messenger of an unchaste heart. And whoever turns his gaze on a woman with a mind conscious of lust should not suppose that what a mind weighed down by sins has conceived is hidden. But suppose it certain that it is hidden, so that it is seen by no human being at all: what will he do about that Watcher whom secrets do not deceive, from whom hidden things cannot be concealed? Let that wounded man, then, fear to displease God, to whom he desires to show himself a faithful servant; let him take thought not to admit into his mind women who would please him wrongly; let him fear that One sees all things, from whom human action can hide nothing. Let the fear of Him, then, be held constantly present, of whom it is written: An abomination to the Lord is one who fixes his eye (Prov. xvi). So when you are together in church, or in any place where women too may be present, each of you, taking care for all, guard your chastity diligently. For God who dwells in you will deign to guard you, when care of this kind is applied. And if anyone notices in one of you this wantonness of the eye of which I speak, warn him at once, so that he may be corrected straight away. Nor should he think himself malicious when he points this out; and for that reason one who is of this kind ought to be made known, lest he grow worse. But if, having been warned, he neglects to amend, it must be reported to the abbot, so that he may undergo corrective discipline from him. But if he does not amend even so, let him be cast out of your fellowship like a diseased sheep, lest by his example he destroy others. For the vice of desire is to be investigated in such a way that, when anyone is recognised to be suffering from this vice, he is chastised by many, with love of neighbour and hatred of vices.

Chapter XIX. Whoever presumes to accept letters or small gifts from anyone, if he does not at once make known from whom he received them and what he received, will be subject to the most severe punishment. And the things that were sent will be assigned to strangers and unknown persons, or else burned in the fire. Certainly, if anyone has given something to his sons, or to any connected to him by kinship, it should be put into common stock and given to whoever has need of it. But if the abbot orders it to be given to the one to whom it was sent, he will receive it with thanksgiving, like the other gifts of the faithful. Care must also be taken that an excessive desire for clean clothing does not bring on inner filth of the soul. Therefore [clothes] are to be washed according to the prior's direction. They are to be provided in so simple and natural a colour that difference of garments does not nourish the vice of arrogance; and they are to be given to those in need in such a way that, [things] being kept back through the vice of avarice, boldness is not given to individuals in providing for themselves. But if anyone thinks these things may be sought carelessly, let it be the prior's care that the embezzler of the monastery's goods be corrected. Above all, take care that you have no quarrels; but if they arise at the devil's prompting, let them be healed by swift amends, and let remedies come forth from the place where the wounds were made; and let not the sun go down upon your anger. Cast off the habit of swearing. Let your speech be yes, yes, no, no (Ephes. iv); for, as the Lord says: What is more than these is from evil (Matth. v).

Chapter XX. Women should not frequent your dwelling; but when they seek out the monastery out of their devotion or out of love for your religious life, they should not be allowed to enter the inner gates of the monastery, but honour and kindness should be shown to them in the oratory or in the guest house: not for the sake of expectation, but in accordance with the ordinance of the rule and the discipline of the monastery.

Chapter XXI. Over those suffering from illnesses or any other infirmity a thoroughly faithful and energetic person should be set, who will both serve the sick with kindness, and keep the monastic discipline according to the rule, and dispense sensibly what is suitable for the sick.

Chapter XXII. Those who are set over the cellar or over the books should serve the brothers without murmuring. Those who ask for books outside the [appointed] hour should not receive them; and those who have with them more than is appointed should not dare to keep them. Doing these things in the name of Christ, you know that you are making progress, and are persevering in the monastery with gentleness and quiet. But when the necessity of discipline in restraining conduct compels you to speak harsh words, even if you perhaps feel that in them you have exceeded the measure of discipline, it is not required of you that you ask pardon: lest, before those who ought to be subject, while humility is overly observed, the authority of governing be broken. Yet pardon must be sought from the Lord of all, who knows with how much goodwill you love even those whom you perhaps rebuke more than is just. For charity, of which it is written that it does not seek what is its own (I Cor. xiii), is understood to be kept here too: for while they strive to humble the pride of others, they cannot humble their persons as much as they wish. For the love between you ought to be not carnal but spiritual; and therefore think the more diligently of the salvation of all: for each one is to render account to the Lord for the souls entrusted to him.

Chapter XXIII. The prior is to be obeyed especially, and much more the abbot, who has the care of you all; for whoever despises them despises him who said: Whoever hears you hears me; whoever despises you despises me (Luke xvii). That all these things, then, may be kept, and that if anything is not kept it is not carelessly passed over but care is taken that it be amended and corrected, will pertain chiefly to the prior; so that he may refer to the abbot, whose authority among you is greater, what exceeds his own measure or strength. And he who is over you should not consider himself happy in ruling power, but in serving charity; in honour let him be preferred before you, before God let him lie at your feet. Towards all let him offer himself as an example of good works. Let him rebuke the restless, console the faint-hearted, support the weak, be patient towards all; let him maintain discipline willingly, and impose fear. And although both are necessary, yet let him seek more to be loved than feared, always considering that he will render account to God for you. Therefore, by obeying the more, have pity not only on yourselves but also on him; for among you, the higher the place he holds, the greater the danger he is in.

May the Lord grant that you observe all these things with love, as lovers of spiritual beauty, and fragrant with the good odour of Christ from a good way of life: not as slaves under the law, but as those established free under grace. And so that you can look at yourselves in this little book as in a mirror, and may not neglect anything through forgetfulness, let it be read to you once a week. And where you find yourselves doing the things that are written, give thanks to God, the giver of all good things; but where any of you sees that something is lacking in himself, let him grieve for the past and be on guard for the future, praying that his debt be forgiven and that he not be led into temptation.
